A specific texture associated with the event

I drift off into a world of my own
make sure never to be alone with another person

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

I feel like an object, not like a person
You can never know who will harm you

Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items
issues.explanation: The profile contains several items implying an active sense of present threat or exposure (e.g., 'World is Dangerous', 'Exposed to Others', concealment to avoid being noticed), yet the Threat component is entirely absent. For this trauma type, such items would usually cohere with at least some explicit threat content; the omission makes the cross-node picture clinically uneven.

'World is Dangerous' expresses a broad ongoing threat belief, but the formulation specifies no active links into or out of Threat and no Threat items are endorsed. This makes the appraisal sit awkwardly in the formulation because it functions more like a threat belief than an isolated negative self-appraisal.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
issues.explanation: 'Concealing Clothing ... to avoid being noticed' implies active management of current interpersonal threat/visibility. With Threat completely unrepresented and no Trigger→Threat or Maladaptive Strategies→Threat linkage in the formulation, this strategy lacks a clear matching symptom target in the rest of the profile.

Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: The Threat node is not clinically coherent here. 'Flashbacks' and 'Physical Reactivity' are re-experiencing/arousal responses rather than threat appraisals, while the only genuine threat appraisal selected is 'Threat from Strangers.' That mixes different constructs within one node.

vignette: Meet 25-year-old Jamal, a housekeeper who has been struggling to come to terms with his traumatic past. As a child, Jamal suffered physical abuse at the hands of his caregiver, an experience that has left an indelible mark on his life. Jamal's days are often marked by a sense of hypervigilance, as if he is constantly on guard against potential threats. He can't shake off the feeling that others can see right through him, that they know about the abuse just by looking at him. This feeling of exposure makes him want to escape, to drift off into his own world where he feels safe. Jamal has developed a coping mechanism - fantasy escape - where he detaches himself from reality and enters a world of his own creation. But this escape is short-lived. The slightest trigger can transport him back to the traumatic event. The sound of children crying, for instance, is enough to set off a chain reaction. Jamal's mind starts racing, and he feels like he's reliving the experience all over again. The memories come flooding back - vivid, full sensory replays that leave him feeling overwhelmed and helpless. When these memories resurface, Jamal tries to give up important responsibilities, hoping to avoid triggers and stay safe. He'll call in sick or abandon tasks halfway through, unable to shake off the feeling of impending doom. His colleagues have noticed this pattern, but Jamal can't explain why he's been so unreliable lately. All he knows is that he needs to escape, to find a way out of the darkness that seems to be closing in on him. As the memories replay in his mind, Jamal starts to feel like an object, not a person. He's convinced that others see him as damaged goods, someone who can never truly be whole again. This dehumanization makes him more withdrawn, more determined to avoid human contact at all costs. Never alone is his new mantra - he'll do whatever it takes to ensure that he's always surrounded by people, even if it means sacrificing his own needs and desires. But this strategy backfires. The more Jamal tries to escape, the more memories resurface. And with each replay, the triggers become more potent, more likely to set off a chain reaction of flashbacks and physical reactivity. It's as if his body is constantly on high alert, waiting for the next threat to emerge. As Jamal navigates this complex web of emotions, he becomes increasingly isolated. His relationships suffer, his work performance declines, and he starts to lose touch with reality. The memories continue to haunt him, replaying like a film that refuses to end. And at the center of it all is the feeling of fear - the certainty that harm can come from anywhere, at any time. It's this sense of hopelessness that finally brings Jamal to seek help. He's exhausted by the constant struggle, the endless cycle of triggers and memories and maladaptive strategies. As he sits in the therapist's office, he knows that he needs to confront his demons head-on. It won't be easy - but for the first time in years, Jamal feels a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, he can learn to overcome his past and find a way forward.
